entries.e998f18cf477d6d65f0e3bab88df7b62bc3992fb: <div sID="gen32235" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="1Thess.5" sID="1Thess.5"/> <div eID="gen32235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32236" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32237" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having spoken in the end of the foregoing chapter concerning the resurrection, and the second coming of Christ, proceeds to speak concerning the uselessness of enquiring after the particular time of Christ's coming, which would be sudden and terrible to the wicked, but comfortable to the saints, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1-1Thess.5.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. He then exhorts them to the duties of watchfulness, sobriety, and the exercise of faith, love, and hope, as being suitable to their state, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6-1Thess.5.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. In the next words he exhorts them to several duties they owed to others, or to one another (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.11-1Thess.5.15">ver. 11-15</reference>), afterwards to several other Christian duties of great importance (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.16-1Thess.5.22">ver. 16-22</reference>), and then concludes this epistle, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23-1Thess.5.28">ver. 23-28</reference>.
entries.3ae5d2a4a427ce46d3dc1680d8dece929bc54110: <div eID="gen32237" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32236" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Coming of Christ. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But of the times and the seasons, brethren, ye have no need that I write unto you. <hi type="super">2</hi> For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night. <hi type="super">3</hi> For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape. <hi type="super">4</hi> But ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief. 5 Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness. <div eID="gen32238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32239" type="x-p"/> In these words observe, <div eID="gen32239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32240" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle tells the Thessalonians it was needless or useless to enquire about the particular time of Christ's coming: <hi type="italic">Of the times and seasons you need not that I write unto you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1">v. 1</reference>. The thing is certain that Christ will come, and there is a certain time appointed for his coming; but there was no need that the apostle should write about this, and therefore he had no revelation given him; nor should they or we enquire into this secret, <hi type="italic">which the Father has reserved in his own power. Of that day and hour knoweth no man.</hi> Christ himself did not reveal this while upon earth; it was not in his commission as the great prophet of the church: nor did he reveal this to his apostles; there was <hi type="italic">no need</hi> of this. There are times and seasons for us to do our work in: these it is our duty and interest to know and observe; but the time and season when we must give up our account we know not, nor is it needful that we should know them. Note, There are many things which our vain curiosity desires to know which there is no necessity at all of our knowing, nor would our knowledge of them do us good. <div eID="gen32240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32241" type="x-p"/> II. He tells them that the coming of Christ would be sudden, and a great surprise to most men, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2">v. 2</reference>. And this is what they knew perfectly, or might know, because our Lord himself had so said: <hi type="italic">In such an hour as you think not, the Son of man cometh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.44">Matt. xxiv. 44</reference>. So <reference osisRef="Mark.13.35-Mark.13.36">Mark xiii. 35, 36</reference>, <hi type="italic">Watch you therefore, for you know not when the master of the house cometh; lest, coming suddenly, he find you sleeping.</hi> And no doubt the apostle had told them, as of the coming of Christ, so also of his coming suddenly, which is the meaning of his coming <hi type="italic">as a thief in the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.16.15">Rev. xvi. 15</reference>. As the thief usually cometh in the dead time of the night, when he is least expected, such a <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> will the day of the Lord be; so sudden and surprising will be his appearance. The knowledge of this will be more useful than to know the exact time, because this should awaken us to stand upon our watch, that we may be ready whenever he cometh. <div eID="gen32241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32242" type="x-p"/> III. He tells them how terrible Christ's coming would be to the ungodly, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">v. 3</reference>. It will be to their destruction in that day of the Lord. The righteous God will bring ruin upon his and his people's enemies; and this their destruction, as it will be total and final, so, 1. It will be sudden. It will overtake them, and fall upon them, in the midst of their carnal security and jollity, when they say in their hearts, <hi type="italic">Peace and safety,</hi> when they dream of felicity and please themselves with vain amusements of their fancies or their senses, and think not of it,—<hi type="italic">as travail cometh upon a woman with child,</hi> at the set time indeed, but not perhaps just then expected, nor greatly feared. 2. It will be unavoidable destruction too: <hi type="italic">They shall not escape;</hi> they shall in no wise escape. There will be no means possible for them to avoid the terror nor the punishment of that day. There will be <hi type="italic">no place where the workers of iniquity shall be able to hide themselves,</hi> no shelter from the storm, nor shadow from the burning heat that shall consume the wicked. <div eID="gen32242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32243" type="x-p"/> IV. He tells them how comfortable this day will be to the righteous, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.4-1Thess.5.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Here observe, 1. Their character and privilege. They are not in darkness; they are the children of the light, &c. This was the happy condition of the Thessalonians as it is of all true Christians. They were not in a state of sin and ignorance as the heathen world. They were <hi type="italic">some time darkness, but were made light in the Lord.</hi> They were favoured with the divine revelation of things that are unseen and eternal, particularly concerning the coming of Christ, and the consequences thereof. They were the <hi type="italic">children of the day,</hi> for the day-star had risen upon them; yea, the Sun of righteousness had arisen on them with healing under his wings. They were no longer under the darkness of heathenism, nor under the shadows of the law, but under the gospel, which brings life and immortality to light. <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2 Tim. i. 10</reference>. 2. Their great advantage on this account: that <hi type="italic">that day should not overtake them as a thief,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.4">v. 4</reference>. It was at least their own fault if they were surprised by that day. They had fair warning, and sufficient helps to provide against that day, and might hope to stand with comfort and confidence before the Son of man. This would be a time of <hi type="italic">refreshing to them from the presence of the Lord,</hi> who to <hi type="italic">those that look for him will appear without sin unto their salvation,</hi> and will come to them as a friend in the day, not as a thief in the night.
entries.fd5d411380748b0cd12fd67a80b3fd5a663338d1: <div eID="gen32243" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Watchfulness and Sobriety. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore let us not sleep, as <hi type="italic">do</hi> others; but let us watch and be sober. <hi type="super">7</hi> For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night. <hi type="super">8</hi> But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for a helmet, the hope of salvation. <hi type="super">9</hi> For God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ, <hi type="super">10</hi> Who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him. <div eID="gen32244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32245" type="x-p"/> On what had been said, the apostle grounds seasonable exhortations to several needful duties. <div eID="gen32245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32246" type="x-p"/> I. To watchfulness and sobriety, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6">v. 6</reference>. These duties are distinct, yet they mutually befriend one another. For, while we are compassed about with so many temptations to intemperance and excess, we shall not keep sober, unless we be upon our guard, and, unless we keep sober, we shall not long watch. 1. Then <hi type="italic">let us not sleep as do others, but let us watch;</hi> we must not be secure and careless, nor indulge spiritual sloth and idleness. We must not be off our watch, but continually upon our guard against sin, and temptation to it. The generality of men are too careless of their duty and regardless of their spiritual enemies. They say, <hi type="italic">Peace and safety,</hi> when they are in the greatest danger, doze away their precious moments on which eternity depends, indulging idle dreams, and have no more thoughts nor cares about another world than men that are asleep have about this. Either they do not consider the things of another world at all, because they are asleep; or they do not consider them aright, because they dream. But let us watch, and act like men that are awake, and that stand upon their guard. 2. Let us also <hi type="italic">be sober,</hi> or temperate and moderate. Let us keep our natural desires and appetites after the things of this world within due bounds. Sobriety is usually opposed to excess in meats and drinks, and here particularly it is opposed to drunkenness; but it also extends to all other temporal things. Thus our Saviour warned his disciples to <hi type="italic">take heed lest their hearts should be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come on them unawares,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.34">Luke xxi. 34</reference>. <hi type="italic">Our moderation</hi> then, as to all temporal things, <hi type="italic">should be known to all men, because the Lord is at hand.</hi> Besides this, watchfulness and sobriety are most suitable to the Christian's character and privilege, as being <hi type="italic">children of the day;</hi> because <hi type="italic">those that sleep sleep in the night, and those that are drunken are drunken in the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.7">v. 7</reference>. It is a most reproachful thing for men to sleep away the day-time, which is for work and not for sleep, to be drunken in the day, when so many eyes are upon them, to behold their shame. It was not so strange if those who had not the benefit of divine revelation suffered themselves to be lulled asleep by the devil in carnal security, and if they laid the reins upon the neck of their appetites, and indulged themselves in all manner of riot and excess; for it was night-time with them. They were not sensible of their danger, therefore they <hi type="italic">slept;</hi> they were not sensible of their duty, therefore they were drunk: but it ill becomes Christians to do thus. What! shall Christians, who have the light of the blessed gospel shining in their faces, be careless about their souls, and unmindful of another world? Those who have so many eyes upon them should conduct themselves with peculiar propriety. <div eID="gen32246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32247" type="x-p"/> II. To be well armed as well as watchful: to put on the whole armour of God. This is necessary in order to such sobriety as becomes us and will be a preparation for the day of the Lord, because our spiritual enemies are many, and mighty, and malicious. They draw many to their interest, and keep them in it, by making them careless, secure, and presumptuous, by making them drunk—drunk with pride, drunk with passion, drunk and giddy with self-conceit, drunk with the gratifications of sense: so that we have need to arm ourselves against their attempts, by putting on the spiritual breast-plate to keep the heart, and the spiritual helmet to secure the head; and this spiritual armour consists of three great graces of Christians, faith, love, and hope, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">v. 8</reference>. 1. We must live by faith, and this will keep us watchful and sober. If we believe that the eye of God (who is a spirit) is always upon us, that we have spiritual enemies to grapple with, that there is a world of spirits to prepare for, we shall see reason to watch and be sober. Faith will be our best defence against the assaults of our enemies. 2. We must get a heart inflamed with love; and this also will be our defence. True and fervent love to God, and the things of God, will keep us watchful and sober, and hinder our apostasy in times of trouble and temptation. 3. We must make salvation our hope, and should have a lively hope of it. This good hope, through grace, of eternal life, will be as a helmet to defend the head, and hinder our being intoxicated with the pleasures of sin, which are but for a season. If we have hope of salvation, let us take heed of doing any thing that shall shake our hopes, or render us unworthy of or unfit for the great salvation we hope for. Having mentioned salvation and the hope of it, the apostle shows what grounds and reasons Christians have to hope for this salvation, as to which observe, He says nothing of their meriting it. No, the doctrine of our merits is altogether unscriptural and antiscriptural; there is no foundation of any good hope upon that account. But our hopes are to be grounded, (1.) Upon God's appointment: because <hi type="italic">God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">v. 9</reference>. If we would trace our salvation to the first cause, that is God's appointment. Those who live and die in darkness and ignorance, who sleep and are drunken as in the night, are, it is but too plain, <hi type="italic">appointed to wrath;</hi> but as for those who are of the day, if they watch and be sober, it is evident that they are <hi type="italic">appointed to obtain salvation.</hi> And the sureness and firmness of the divine appointment are the great support and encouragement of our hope. Were we to obtain salvation by our own merit or power, we could have but little or no hope of it; but seeing we are to obtain it by virtue of God's appointment, which we are sure cannot be shaken (<hi type="italic">for his purpose, according to election, shall stand</hi>), on this we build unshaken hope, especially when we consider, (2.) Christ's merit and grace, and that salvation is by our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us. Our salvation therefore is owing to, and our hopes of it are grounded on, Christ's atonement as well as God's appointment: and, as we should think on God's gracious design and purpose, so also on Christ's death and sufferings, for this end, <hi type="italic">that whether we wake or sleep</hi> (whether we live or die, for death is but a sleep to believers, as the apostles had before intimated) <hi type="italic">we should live together with Christ</hi> live in union and in glory with him for ever. And, as it is the salvation that Christians hope for to <hi type="italic">be for ever with the Lord,</hi> so one foundation of their hope is their union with him. And if they are united with Christ, and live in him, and live to him, here, the sleep of death will be no prejudice to the spiritual life, much less to the life of glory hereafter. On the contrary, Christ died for us, that, living and dying, we might be his; that we might live to him while we are here, and live with him when we go hence.
entries.1899a49a44b878e6fadc60eb15eff273689f9a82: <div eID="gen32247" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Exhortations; Duty towards Fellow-Christians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32248" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do. <hi type="super">12</hi> And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; <hi type="super">13</hi> And to esteem them very highly in love for their work's sake. <hi type="italic">And</hi> be at peace among yourselves. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> See that none render evil for evil unto any <hi type="italic">man;</hi> but ever follow that which is good, both among yourselves, and to all <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <div eID="gen32248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32249" type="x-p"/> In these words the apostle exhorts the Thessalonians to several duties. <div eID="gen32249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32250" type="x-p"/> I. Towards those who were nearly related one to another. Such should comfort themselves, or exhort one another, and edify one another, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.11">v. 11</reference>. 1. They must comfort or exhort themselves and one another; for the original word may be rendered both these ways. And we may observe, As those are most able and likely to comfort others who can comfort themselves, so the way to have comfort ourselves, or to administer comfort to others, is by compliance with the exhortation of the word. Note, We should not only be careful about our own comfort and welfare, but to promote the comfort and welfare of others also. He was a Cain that said, <hi type="italic">Am I my brother's keeper?</hi> We <hi type="italic">must bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.</hi> 2. They must edify one another, by <hi type="italic">following after those things whereby one may edify another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.14.19">Rom. xiv. 19</reference>. As Christians are lively stones built up together a spiritual house, they should endeavour to promote the good of the whole church by promoting the work of grace in one another. And it is the duty of every one of us to study that which is for the edification of those with whom we converse, <hi type="italic">to please all men for their</hi> real <hi type="italic">profit.</hi> We should communicate our knowledge and experiences one to another. We should join in prayer and praise one with another. We should set a good example one before another. And it is the duty of those especially who live in the same vicinity and family thus to comfort and edify one another; and this is the best neighbourhood, the best means to answer the end of society. Such as are nearly related together and have affection for one another, as they have the greatest opportunity, so they are under the greatest obligation, to do this kindness one to another. This the Thessalonians did (<hi type="italic">which also you do</hi>), and this is what they are exhorted to continue and increase in doing. Note, Those who do that which is good have need of further exhortations to excite them to do good, to do more good, as well as continue in doing what they do. <div eID="gen32250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32251" type="x-p"/> II. He shows them their duty towards their ministers, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12-1Thess.5.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Though the apostle himself was driven from them, yet they had others who laboured among them, and to whom they owed these duties. The apostle here exhorts them to observe, <div eID="gen32251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32252" type="x-p"/> 1. How the ministers of the gospel are described by the work of their office; and they should rather mind the work and duty they are called to than affect venerable and honourable names that they may be called by. Their work is very weighty, and very honourable and useful. (1.) Ministers must labour among their people, labour with diligence, and unto weariness (so the word in the original imports); <hi type="italic">they must labour in the word and doctrine,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1 Tim. v. 17</reference>. They are called labourers, and should not be loiterers. They must labour with their people, to instruct, comfort, and edify them. And, (2.) Ministers are to rule their people also, so the word is rendered, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1 Tim. v. 17</reference>. They must rule, not with rigour, but with love. They must not exercise dominion as temporal lords; but rule as spiritual guides, by setting a good example to the flock. They are over the people in the Lord, to distinguish them from civil magistrates, and to denote also that they are but ministers under Christ, appointed by him, and must rule the people by Christ's laws, and not by laws of their own. This may also intimate the end of their office and all their labour; namely, the service and honour of the Lord. (3.) They must also admonish the people, and that not only publicly, but privately, as there may be occasion. They must instruct them to do well, and should reprove when they do ill. It is their duty not only to give good counsel, but also to give admonition, to give warning to the flock of the dangers they are liable to, and reprove for negligence or what else may be amiss. <div eID="gen32252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32253" type="x-p"/> 2. What the duty of the people is towards their ministers. There is a mutual duty between ministers and people. If ministers should labour among the people, then, (1.) The people must know them. As the shepherd should know his flock, so the sheep must know their shepherd. They must know his person, hear his voice, acknowledge him for their pastor, and pay due regard to his teaching, ruling, and admonitions. (2.) They must esteem their ministers highly in love; they should greatly value the office of the ministry, honour and love the persons of their ministers, and show their esteem and affection in all proper ways, and this for their work's sake, because their business is to promote the honour of Christ and the welfare of men's souls. Note, Faithful ministers ought to be so far from being lightly esteemed because of their work that they should be highly esteemed on account of it. The work of the ministry is so far from being a disgrace to those who upon other accounts deserve esteem, that it puts an honour upon those who are faithful and diligent, to which otherwise they could lay no claim, and will procure them that esteem and love among good people which otherwise they could not expect. <div eID="gen32253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32254" type="x-p"/> III. He gives divers other exhortations touching the duty Christians owe to one another. 1. To <hi type="italic">be at peace among themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.13">v. 13</reference>. Some understand this exhortation (according to the reading in some copies) as referring to the people's duty to their ministers, to live peaceably with them, and not raise nor promote dissensions at any time between minister and people, which will certainly prove a hindrance to the success of a minister's work and the edification of the people. This is certain, that ministers and people should avoid every thing that tends to alienate their affections one from another. And the people should be at peace among themselves, doing all they can to hinder any differences from rising or continuing among them, and using all proper means to preserve peace and harmony. 2. <hi type="italic">To warn the unruly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">v. 14</reference>. There will be in all societies some who walk disorderly, who go out of their rank and station; and it is not only the duty of ministers, but of private Christians also, to warn and admonish them. Such should be reproved for their sin, warned of their danger, and told plainly of the injury they do their own souls, and the hurt they may do to others. Such should be put in mind of what they should do, and be reproved for doing otherwise. 3. <hi type="italic">To comfort the feebleminded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">v. 14</reference>. By these are intended the timorous and faint-hearted, or such as are dejected and of a sorrowful spirit. Some are cowardly, afraid of difficulties, and disheartened at the thoughts of hazards, and losses, and afflictions; now such should be encouraged; we should not despise them, but comfort them; and who knows what good a kind and comfortable word may do them? 4. <hi type="italic">To support the weak,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">v. 14</reference>. Some are not well able to perform their work, nor bear up under their burdens; we should therefore support them, help their infirmities, and lift at one end of the burden, and so help to bear it. It is the grace of God, indeed, that must strengthen and support such; but we should tell them of that grace, and endeavour to minister of that grace to them. 5. <hi type="italic">To be patient towards all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">v. 14</reference>. We must bear and forbear. We must be long-suffering, and suppress our anger, if it begin to rise upon the apprehension of affronts or injuries; at least we must not fail to moderate our anger: and this duty must be exercised towards all men, good and bad, high and low. We must not be high in our expectations and demands, nor harsh in our resentments, nor hard in our impositions, but endeavour to make the best we can of every thing, and think the best we can of every body. 6. <hi type="italic">Not to render evil for evil to any man,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.15">v. 15</reference>. This we must look to, and be very careful about, that is, we must by all means forbear to avenge ourselves. If others do us an injury, this will not justify us in returning it, in doing the same, or the like, or any other injury to them. It becomes us to forgive, as those that are, and that hope to be, forgiven of God. 7. <hi type="italic">Ever to follow that which is good,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.15">v. 15</reference>. In general, we must study to do what is our duty, and pleasing to God, in all circumstances, whether men do us good turns or ill turns; whatever men do to us, we must do good to others. We must always endeavour to be beneficent and instrumental to promote the welfare of others, both among ourselves (in the first place to those that <hi type="italic">are of the household o faith</hi>), and then, <hi type="italic">as we have opportunity, unto all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.10">Gal. vi. 10</reference>.
entries.6b8589a020f9a44f6ef3da8a86838df0fea35537: <div eID="gen32254" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Short Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Rejoice evermore. <hi type="super">17</hi> Pray without ceasing. <hi type="super">18</hi> In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. <hi type="super">19</hi> Quench not the Spirit. <hi type="super">20</hi> Despise not prophesyings. <hi type="super">21</hi> Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. <hi type="super">22</hi> Abstain from all appearance of evil. <div eID="gen32255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32256" type="x-p"/> Here we have divers short exhortations, that will not burden our memories, but will be of great use to direct the motions of our hearts and lives; for the duties are of great importance, and we may observe how they are connected together, and have a dependence upon one another. 1. <hi type="italic">Rejoice evermore,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.16">v. 16</reference>. This must be understood of spiritual joy; for we must rejoice in our creature-comforts as if we rejoiced not, and must not expect to live many years, and rejoice in them all; but, if we do rejoice in God, we may do that evermore. In him our joy will be full; and it is our fault if we have not a continual feast. If we are sorrowful upon any worldly account, yet still we may always rejoice, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. Note, A religious life is a pleasant life, it is a life of constant joy. 2. <hi type="italic">Pray without ceasing,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.17">v. 17</reference>. Note, The way to rejoice evermore is to pray without ceasing. We should rejoice more if we prayed more. We should keep up stated times for prayer, and continue instant in prayer. We should pray always, and not faint: pray without weariness, and continue in prayer, till we come to that world where prayer shall be swallowed up in praise. The meaning is not that men should do nothing but pray, but that nothing else we do should hinder prayer in its proper season. Prayer will help forward and not hinder all other lawful business, and every good work. 3. <hi type="italic">In every thing give thanks,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">v. 18</reference>. If we pray without ceasing, we shall not want matter for thanksgiving <hi type="italic">in every thing.</hi> As we must in every thing make our requests known to God by supplications, so we must not omit thanksgiving, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Phil. iv. 6</reference>. We should be thankful in every condition, even in adversity as well as prosperity. It is never so bad with us but it might be worse. If we have ever so much occasion to make our humble complaints to God, we never can have any reason to complain of God, and have always much reason to praise and give thanks: the apostle says, This is the <hi type="italic">will of God in Christ Jesus concerning us, that we give thanks,</hi> seeing God is reconciled to us in Christ Jesus; in him, through him, and for his sake, he allows us to rejoice evermore, and appoints us in every thing to give thanks. It is pleasing to God. 4. <hi type="italic">Quench not the Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.19">v. 19</reference>), for it is this Spirit of grace and supplication that helpeth our infirmities, that assisteth us in our prayers and thanksgivings. Christians are said to <hi type="italic">be baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire.</hi> He worketh as fire, by enlightening, enlivening, and purifying the souls of men. We must be careful not to quench this holy fire. As fire is put out by withdrawing fuel, so we quench the Spirit if we do not stir up our spirits, and all that is within us, to comply with the motions of the good Spirit; and as fire is quenched by pouring water, or putting a great quantity of dirt upon it, so we must be careful not to quench the Holy Spirit by indulging carnal lusts and affections, or minding only earthly things. 5. <hi type="italic">Despise not prophesyings</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.20">v. 20</reference>); for, if we neglect the means of grace, we forfeit the Spirit of grace. By <hi type="italic">prophesyings</hi> here we are to understand the preaching of the word, the interpreting and applying of the scriptures; and this we must not despise, but should prize and value, because it is the ordinance of God, appointed of him for our furtherance and increase in knowledge and grace, in holiness and comfort. We must not despise preaching, though it be plain, and not with enticing words of men's wisdom, and though we be told no more than what we knew before. It is useful, and many times needful, to have our minds stirred up, our affections and resolutions excited, to those things that we knew before to be our interest and our duty. 6. <hi type="italic">Prove all things, but hold fast that which is good,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">v. 21</reference>. This is a needful caution, to prove all things; for, though we must put a value on preaching, we must not take things upon trust from the preacher, but try them by the law and the testimony. We must search the scriptures, whether what they say be true or not. We must not believe every spirit, but must try the spirits. But we must not be always trying, always unsettled; no, at length we must be settled, and hold fast that which is good. When we are satisfied that any thing is right, and true, and good, we must hold it fast, and not let it go, whatever opposition or whatever persecution we meet with for the sake thereof. Note, The doctrines of human infallibility, implicit faith, and blind obedience, are not the doctrines of the Bible. Every Christian has and ought to have, the judgment of discretion, and should have <hi type="italic">his senses exercised in discerning between good and evil,</hi> truth and falsehood, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.13-Heb.5.14">Heb. v. 13, 14</reference>. And proving all things must be in order to holding fast that which is good. We must not always be seekers, or fluctuating in our minds, <hi type="italic">like children tossed to and fro with every wind of doctrine.</hi> 7. <hi type="italic">Abstain from all appearance of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.22">v. 22</reference>. This is a good means to prevent our being deceived with false doctrines, or unsettled in our faith; for our Saviour has told us (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">If a man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God.</hi> Corrupt affections indulged in the heart, and evil practices allowed of in the life, will greatly tend to promote fatal errors in the mind; whereas purity of heart, and integrity of life, will dispose men to receive the truth in the love of it. We should therefore abstain from evil, and all appearances of evil, from sin, and that which looks like sin, leads to it, and borders upon it. He who is not shy of the appearances of sin, who shuns not the occasions of sin, and who avoids not the temptations and approaches to sin, will not long abstain from the actual commission of sin.
entries.a2fdc99f1fcadb4bf1e3ba44d9281a8675eb792b: <div eID="gen32256" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Prayer for the Thessalonians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32257" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and <hi type="italic">I pray God</hi> your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Faithful <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that calleth you, who also will do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> Brethren, pray for us. <hi type="super">26</hi> Greet all the brethren with a holy kiss. <hi type="super">27</hi> I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren. <hi type="super">28</hi> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you. Amen. <div eID="gen32257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32258" type="x-p"/> In these words, which conclude this epistle, observe, <div eID="gen32258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32259" type="x-p"/> I. Paul's prayer for them, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">v. 23</reference>. He had told them, in the beginning of this epistle, that he always made mention of them in his prayers; and, now that he is writing to them, he lifts up his heart to God in prayer for them. Take notice, 1. To whom the apostle prays, namely, <hi type="italic">The very God of peace.</hi> He is the God of grace, and the God of peace and love. He is the author of peace and lover of concord; and by their peaceableness and unity, from God as the author, those things would best be obtained which he prays for. 2. The things he prays for on behalf of the Thessalonians are their sanctification, that <hi type="italic">God would sanctify them wholly;</hi> and their preservation, that they might be <hi type="italic">preserved blameless.</hi> He prays that they may be wholly sanctified, that the whole man may be sanctified, and then that the whole man, spirit, soul, and body, may be preserved: or, he prays that they may be wholly sanctified, that is, more perfectly, for the best are sanctified but in part while in this world; and therefore we should pray for and press towards complete sanctification. Where the good work of grace is begun, it shall be carried on, be protected and preserved; and all those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus shall be preserved to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. And because, if God did not carry on his good work in the soul, it would miscarry, we should pray to God to perfect his work, and <hi type="italic">preserve us blameless,</hi> free from sin and impurity, till at length we are <hi type="italic">presented faultless before the throne of his glory with exceeding joy.</hi> <div eID="gen32259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32260" type="x-p"/> II. His comfortable assurance that God would hear his prayer: <hi type="italic">Faithful is he who calleth you, who will also do it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.24">v. 24</reference>. The kindness and love of God had appeared to them in calling them to the knowledge of his truth, and the faithfulness of God was their security that they should persevere to the end; and therefore, the apostle assures them, God would do what he desired; he would effect what he had promised; he would accomplish all the good pleasure of his goodness towards them. Note, Our fidelity to God depends upon his faithfulness to us. <div eID="gen32260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32261" type="x-p"/> III. His request of their prayers: <hi type="italic">Brethren, pray for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.25">v. 25</reference>. We should pray for one another; and brethren should thus express brotherly love. This great apostle did not think it beneath him to call the Thessalonians brethren, nor to request their prayers. Ministers stand in need of their people's prayers; and the more people pray for their ministers the more good ministers may have from God, and the more benefit people may receive by their ministry. <div eID="gen32261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32262" type="x-p"/> IV. His salutation: <hi type="italic">Greet all the brethren with a holy kiss,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.26">v. 26</reference>. Thus the apostle sends a friendly salutation from himself, and Silvanus, and Timotheus, and would have them salute each other in their names; and thus he would have them signify their mutual love and affection to one another by the kiss of charity (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.14">1 Pet. v. 14</reference>), which is here called a holy kiss, to intimate how cautious they should be of all impurity in the use of this ceremony, then commonly practised; as it should not be a treacherous kiss like that of Judas, so not a lascivious kiss like that of the harlot, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Prov. vii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen32262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32263" type="x-p"/> V. His solemn charge for the reading of this epistle, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">v. 27</reference>. This is not only an exhortation, but an adjuration by the Lord. And this epistle was to be read to all the holy brethren. It is not only allowed to the common people to read the scriptures, and what none should prohibit, but it is their indispensable duty, and what they should be persuaded to do. In order to this, these holy oracles should not be kept concealed in an unknown tongue, but translated into the vulgar languages, that all men, being concerned to know the scriptures, may be able to read them, and be acquainted with them. The public reading of the law was one part of the worship of the sabbath among the Jews in their synagogues, and the scriptures should be read in the public assemblies of Christians also. <div eID="gen32263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32264" type="x-p"/> VI. The apostolical benediction that is usual in other epistles: <hi type="italic">The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.28">v. 28</reference>. We need no more to make us happy than to know that grace which our Lord Jesus Christ has manifested, be interested in that grace which he has purchased, and partake of that grace which dwells in him as the head of the church. This is an ever-flowing and overflowing fountain of grace to supply all our wants.  <chapter eID="1Thess.5"/> <div eID="gen32264" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32140" osisID="1Thess" type="book"/>

entries.4a20b8202b6036c523395d6ec60e5771bc2c55f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17981"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen36796" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1-1Thess.5.28">1Th 5:1-28</reference>. The Suddenness of Christ's Coming a Motive for Watchfulness; Various Precepts: Prayer for Their Being Found Blameless, Body, Soul, and Spirit, at Christ's Coming: Conclusion.<div eID="gen36796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17981"/><hi type="bold">1. times--</hi>the general and indefinite term for chronological periods.<div eID="gen36797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seasons--</hi>the opportune times (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">Da 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>). Time denotes quantity; season, quality. Seasons are parts of times.<div eID="gen36798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye have no need--</hi>those who watch do not need to be told when the hour will come, for they are always ready [Bengel].<div eID="gen36799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh--</hi>present: expressing its speedy and awful certainty. <div eID="gen36800" type="x-p"/>
entries.36e116737b7a32a846281d6783b2fa25aaca615d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17982"/><div sID="gen36801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17982"/><hi type="bold">2. as a thief in the night--</hi>The apostles in this image follow the parable of their Lord, expressing how the Lord's coming shall take men by surprise (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.43">Mt 24:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>). "The night is wherever there is quiet unconcern" [Bengel]. "At midnight" (perhaps figurative: to some parts of the earth it will be literal night), <reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Mt 25:6</reference>. The thief not only gives no notice of his approach but takes all precaution to prevent the household knowing of it. So the Lord (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.15">Re 16:15</reference>). Signs will precede the coming, to confirm the patient hope of the watchful believer; but the coming itself shall be sudden at last (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.32-Matt.24.36">Mt 24:32-36</reference>; Lu 21:25-32, 35). <div eID="gen36801" type="x-p"/>
entries.c09b7571bc9ed1d20216769cac46a82d249ac87a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17983"/><div sID="gen36802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17983"/><hi type="bold">3. they--</hi>the men of the world. <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">1Th 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>, "others," all the rest of the world save Christians.<div eID="gen36802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.18.7">Jud 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.9.27">9, 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.9.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jr 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>).<div eID="gen36803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>at the very moment when they least expect it. Compare the case of Belshazzar, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.6">Da 5:1-5, 6</reference>, 9, 26-28; Herod, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.21-Acts.12.23">Ac 12:21-23</reference>.<div eID="gen36804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sudden--</hi>"unawares" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.34">Lu 21:34</reference>).<div eID="gen36805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as travail--</hi>"As the labor pang" comes in an instant on the woman when otherwise engaged (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.6">Psa 48:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Is 13:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not escape--</hi>Greek, "shall not at all escape." Another awful feature of their ruin: there shall be then no possibility of shunning it however they desire it (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">Am 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Re 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen36807" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbec450afabe16165b74d6e42a604a5ae8ff896d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17984"/><div sID="gen36808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17984"/><hi type="bold">4. not in darkness--</hi>not in darkness of understanding (that is, spiritual ignorance) or of the moral nature (that is, a state of sin), <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>.<div eID="gen36808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>Greek, "in order that"; with God results are all purposed.<div eID="gen36809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that day--</hi>Greek, "THE day"; the day of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>, "the day"), in contrast to "darkness."<div eID="gen36810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overtake--</hi>unexpectedly (compare <reference osisRef="John.12.35">Joh 12:35</reference>).<div eID="gen36811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a thief--</hi>The two oldest manuscripts read, "as (the daylight overtakes) thieves" (<reference osisRef="Job.24.17">Job 24:17</reference>). Old manuscripts and Vulgate read as English Version. <div eID="gen36812" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cc2358433b48c95e9730a3378a8dd62ec2c4524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17985"/><div sID="gen36813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17985"/>5. The oldest manuscripts read, "FOR ye are all," &c. Ye have no reason for fear, or for being taken by surprise, by the coming of the day of the Lord: "For ye are all sons (so the Greek) of light and sons of day"; a Hebrew idiom, implying that as sons resemble their fathers, so you are in character light (intellectually and morally illuminated in a spiritual point of view), <reference osisRef="Luke.16.8">Lu 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.36">Joh 12:36</reference>.<div eID="gen36813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are not of--</hi>that is, belong not to night nor darkness. The change of person from "ye" to "we" implies this: Ye are sons of light because ye are Christians; and we, Christians, are not of night nor darkness. <div eID="gen36814" type="x-p"/>
entries.4235ea5cd06d5787cdc6c7e780b77814f0a40e98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17986"/><div sID="gen36815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17986"/><hi type="bold">6. others--</hi>Greek, "the rest" of the world: the unconverted (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>). "Sleep" here is worldly apathy to spiritual things (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>); in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.7">1Th 5:7</reference>, ordinary sleep; in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.10">1Th 5:10</reference>, death.<div eID="gen36815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch--</hi>for Christ's coming; literally, "be wakeful." The same Greek occurs in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.34">1Co 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.26">2Ti 2:26</reference>.<div eID="gen36816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be sober--</hi>refraining from carnal indulgence, mental or sensual (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen36817" type="x-p"/>
entries.897e79b9febe364f5711bf561a1c20ac41a4dc2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17987"/><div sID="gen36818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17987"/>7. This verse is to be taken in the literal sense. Night is the time when sleepers sleep, and drinking men are drunk. To sleep by day would imply great indolence; to be drunken by day, great shamelessness. Now, in a spiritual sense, "we Christians profess to be day people, not night people; therefore our work ought to be day work, not night work; our conduct such as will bear the eye of day, and such has no need of the veil of night" [Edmunds], (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen36818" type="x-p"/>
entries.235c323b90ecfddf32c4400ccbd45c801c026c92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17988"/><div sID="gen36819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17988"/>8. Faith, hope, and love, are the three pre-eminent graces (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>). We must not only be awake and sober, but also armed; not only watchful, but also guarded. The armor here is only defensive; in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13-Eph.6.17">Ep 6:13-17</reference>, also offensive. Here, therefore, the reference is to the Christian means of being guarded against being surprised by the day of the Lord as a thief in the night. The helmet and breastplate defend the two vital parts, the head and the heart respectively. "With head and heart right, the whole man is right" [Edmunds]. The head needs to be kept from error, the heart from sin. For "the breastplate of righteousness," <reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">Ep 6:14</reference>, we have here "the breastplate of faith and love"; for the righteousness which is imputed to man for justification, is "faith working by love" (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.22-Rom.4.24">22-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>). "Faith," as the motive within, and "love," exhibited in outward acts, constitute the perfection of righteousness. In <reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">Ep 6:17</reference> the helmet is "salvation"; here, "the hope of salvation." In one aspect "salvation" is a present possession (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.24">5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.13">1Jo 5:13</reference>); in another, it is a matter of "hope" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.24">Ro 8:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">25</reference>). Our Head primarily wore the "breastplate of righteousness" and "helmet of salvation," that we might, by union with Him, receive both. <div eID="gen36819" type="x-p"/>
entries.947f13b4944d813f5091dc64cb68191558d8f0c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17989"/><div sID="gen36820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17989"/><hi type="bold">9. For--</hi>assigning the ground of our "hopes" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed us--</hi>Translate, "set" (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">Ac 13:47</reference>), in His everlasting purpose of love (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1Th 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Ro 9:22</reference>; Jude 4.<div eID="gen36821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to--</hi>that is, unto wrath.<div eID="gen36822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to obtain--</hi>Greek, "to the acquisition of salvation"; said, according to Bengel, Of One saved out of a general wreck, when all things else have been lost: so of the elect saved out of the multitude of the lost (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>). The fact of God's "appointment" of His grace "through Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>), takes away the notion of our being able to "acquire" salvation of ourselves. Christ "acquired (so the Greek for 'purchased') the Church (and its salvation) with His own blood" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>); each member is said to be appointed by God to the "acquiring of salvation." In the primary sense, God does the work; in the secondary sense, man does it. <div eID="gen36823" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d10b4654bf8ccf8d158c383886c6cee3d4642bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17990"/><div sID="gen36824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17990"/><hi type="bold">10. died for us--</hi>Greek, "in our behalf."<div eID="gen36824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whether we wake or sleep--</hi>whether we be found at Christ's coming awake, that is, alive, or asleep, that is, in our graves.<div eID="gen36825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">together--</hi>all of us together; the living not preceding the dead in their glorification "with Him" at His coming (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen36826" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0e580f83b67c0788e01c45bcd990ca1872296f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17991"/><div sID="gen36827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17991"/><hi type="bold">11. comfort yourselves--</hi>Greek, "one another." Here he reverts to the same consolatory strain as in <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.18">1Th 4:18</reference>.<div eID="gen36827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">edify one another--</hi>rather as Greek, "edify (ye) the one the other"; "edify," literally, "build up," namely, in faith, hope, and love, by discoursing together on such edifying topics as the Lord's coming, and the glory of the saints (Mal 3:16). <div eID="gen36828" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ed453a09d7d4703840404c89383423e458eeb92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17992"/><div sID="gen36829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17992"/><hi type="bold">12. beseech--</hi>"Exhort" is the expression in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">1Th 5:14</reference>; here, "we beseech you," as if it were a personal favor (Paul making the cause of the Thessalonian presbyters, as it were, his own).<div eID="gen36829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know--</hi>to have a regard and respect for. Recognize their office, and treat them accordingly (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.18">1Co 16:18</reference>) with reverence and with liberality in supplying their needs (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>). The Thessalonian Church having been newly planted, the ministers were necessarily novices (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.6">1Ti 3:6</reference>), which may have been in part the cause of the people's treating them with less respect. Paul's practice seems to have been to ordain elders in every Church soon after its establishment (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">Ac 14:23</reference>).<div eID="gen36830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them which labour ... are over ... admonish you--</hi>not three classes of ministers, but one, as there is but one article common to the three in the Greek. "Labor" expresses their laborious life; "are over you," their pre-eminence as presidents or superintendents ("bishops," that is, overseers, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>, "them that have rule over you," literally, leaders, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>; "pastors," literally, shepherds, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Ep 4:11</reference>); "admonish you," one of their leading functions; the Greek is "put in mind," implying not arbitrary authority, but gentle, though faithful, admonition (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>, 24, 25; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.3">1Pe 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>Their presidency over you is in divine things; not in worldly affairs, but in things appertaining to the Lord. <div eID="gen36832" type="x-p"/>
entries.db52c1bba8c40b873791e6b4d78666c5a99228d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17993"/><div sID="gen36833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17993"/><hi type="bold">13. very highly--</hi>Greek, "exceeding abundantly."<div eID="gen36833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for their work's sake--</hi>The high nature of their work alone, the furtherance of your salvation and of the kingdom of Christ, should be a sufficient motive to claim your reverential love. At the same time, the word "work," teaches ministers that, while claiming the reverence due to their office, it is not a sinecure, but a "work"; compare "labor" (even to weariness: so the Greek), <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>.<div eID="gen36834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be at peace among yourselves--</hi>The "and" is not in the original. Let there not only be peace between ministers and their flocks, but also no party rivalries among yourselves, one contending in behalf of some one favorite minister, another in behalf of another (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.50">Mr 9:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.6">4:6</reference>). <div eID="gen36835" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f4e5455ba5557c165fbf48e972ba91422db4b78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17994"/><div sID="gen36836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17994"/><hi type="bold">14. brethren--</hi>This exhortation to "warm (Greek, 'admonish,' as in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>) the unruly (those 'disorderly' persons, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">2Th 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">11</reference>, who would not work, and yet expected to be maintained, literally, said of soldiers who will not remain in their ranks, compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">1Th 4:11</reference>; also those insubordinate as to Church discipline, in relation to those 'over' the Church, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>), comfort the feeble-minded (the faint-hearted, who are ready to sink 'without hope' in afflictions, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>, and temptations)," applies to all clergy and laity alike, though primarily the duty of the clergy (who are meant in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>)."<div eID="gen36836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">support--</hi>literally, "lay fast hold on so as to support."<div eID="gen36837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the weak--</hi>spiritually. Paul practiced what he preached (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">1Co 9:22</reference>).<div eID="gen36838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be patient toward all men--</hi>There is no believer who needs not the exercise of patience "toward" him; there is none to whom a believer ought not to show it; many show it more to strangers than to their own families, more to the great than to the humble; but we ought to show it "toward all men" [Bengel]. Compare "the long-suffering of our Lord" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1">2Co 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.15">2Pe 3:15</reference>). <div eID="gen36839" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c07eefca286ed9993dc3db9ece89a37f08265cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17995"/><div sID="gen36840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17995"/>15. (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.17">Ro 12:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1Pe 3:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen36840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto any man--</hi>whether unto a Christian, or a heathen, however great the provocation.<div eID="gen36841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">follow--</hi>as a matter of earnest pursuit. <div eID="gen36842" type="x-p"/>
entries.646c2a1cc0fc2974b37f314f05c4d787e3b9e530: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17996"/><div sID="gen36843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17996"/>16-17. In order to "rejoice evermore," we must "pray without ceasing" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.17">1Th 5:17</reference>). He who is wont to thank God for all things as happening for the best, will have continuous joy [Theophylact]. <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Ep 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">Php 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">6</reference>, "Rejoice in the Lord ... by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving"; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>, "in the Holy Ghost"; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.12">Ro 12:12</reference>, "in hope"; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Ac 5:41</reference>, "in being counted worthy to suffer shame for Christ's name"; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>, in falling "into divers temptations." <div eID="gen36843" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea4076118f7a5cf7c09470419aacbf1fcba8ca8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17998"/><div sID="gen36845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17998"/><hi type="bold">18. In every thing--</hi>even what seems adverse: for nothing is really so (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">Ep 5:20</reference>). See Christ's example (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.36">Mt 15:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.27">26:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Lu 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.11.41">Joh 11:41</reference>).<div eID="gen36845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>That ye should "rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, (and) in every thing give thanks," "is the will of God in Christ Jesus (as the Mediator and Revealer of that will, observed by those who are in Christ by faith, compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">Php 3:14</reference>) concerning you." God's will is the believer's law. Lachmann rightly reads commas at the end of the three precepts (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.16-1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:16-18</reference>), making "this" refer to all three. <div eID="gen36846" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cd0613a5bfe8c8134cd999fb331e9bd3584ef2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17999"/><div sID="gen36847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17999"/><hi type="bold">19. Quench not--</hi>the Spirit being a holy fire: "where the Spirit is, He burns" [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.3">Ac 2:3</reference>; 7:51). Do not throw cold water on those who, under extraordinary inspiration of the Spirit, stand up to speak with tongues, or reveal mysteries, or pray in the congregation. The enthusiastic exhibitions of some (perhaps as to the nearness of Christ's coming, exaggerating Paul's statement, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>, By spirit), led others (probably the presiding ministers, who had not always been treated with due respect by enthusiastic novices, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>), from dread of enthusiasm, to discourage the free utterances of those really inspired, in the Church assembly. On the other hand, the caution (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1Th 5:21</reference>) was needed, not to receive "all" pretended revelations as divine, without "proving" them. <div eID="gen36847" type="x-p"/>
entries.cccb9ed9b08998c0d1e8ca4fab5b0894c052a1ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18000"/><div sID="gen36848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18000"/><hi type="bold">20. prophesyings--</hi>whether exercised in inspired teaching, or in predicting the future. "Despised" by some as beneath "tongues," which seemed most miraculous; therefore declared by Paul to be a greater gift than tongues, though the latter were more showy (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.5">1Co 14:5</reference>). <div eID="gen36848" type="x-p"/>
entries.607a6d269e072cbfb09c24fdc358f1319d5c923e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18001"/><div sID="gen36849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18001"/>21-22. Some of the oldest manuscripts insert "But." You ought indeed not to "quench" the manifestations of "the Spirit," nor "despise prophesyings"; "but," at the same time, do not take "all" as genuine which professes to be so; "prove (test) all" such manifestations. The means of testing them existed in the Church, in those who had the "discerning of spirits" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.29">14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1Jo 4:1</reference>). Another sure test, which we also have, is, to try the professed revelation whether it accords with Scripture, as the noble Bereans did (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.20">Is 8:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>). This precept negatives the Romish priest's assumption of infallibly laying down the law, without the laity having the right, in the exercise of private judgment, to test it by Scripture. Locke says, Those who are for laying aside reason in matters of revelation, resemble one who would put out his eyes in order to use a telescope.<div eID="gen36849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hold fast that which is good--</hi>Join this clause with the next clause (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.22">1Th 5:22</reference>), not merely with the sentence preceding. As the result of your "proving all things," and especially all prophesyings, "hold fast (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.15">Lu 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1Co 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.1">He 2:1</reference>) the good, and hold yourselves aloof from every appearance of evil" ("every evil species" [Bengel and Wahl]). Do not accept even a professedly spirit-inspired communication, if it be at variance with the truth taught you (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36850" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d62813b5d93e9ddd918f37faef279e7fd50eff9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18003"/><div sID="gen36852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18003"/><hi type="bold">23. the very God--</hi>rather as the Greek, "the God of peace Himself"; who can do for you by His own power what I cannot do by all my monitions, nor you by all your efforts (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">Ro 16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.20">He 13:20</reference>), namely, keep you from all evil, and give you all that is good.<div eID="gen36852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctify you--</hi>for holiness is the necessary condition of "peace" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6-Phil.4.9">Php 4:6-9</reference>).<div eID="gen36853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wholly--</hi>Greek, "(so that you should be) perfect in every respect" [Tittmann].<div eID="gen36854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>that is, "and so (omit 'I pray God'; not in the Greek) may your ... spirit and soul and body be preserved," &c.<div eID="gen36855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whole--</hi>A different Greek word from "wholly." Translate, "entire"; with none of the integral parts wanting [Tittmann]. It refers to man in his normal integrity, as originally designed; an ideal which shall be attained by the glorified believer. All three, spirit, soul, and body, each in its due place, constitute man "entire." The "spirit" links man with the higher intelligences of heaven, and is that highest part of man which is receptive of the quickening Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.47">1Co 15:47</reference>). In the unspiritual, the spirit is so sunk under the lower animal soul (which it ought to keep under) that such are termed "animal" (English Version. "sensual," having merely the body of organized matter, and the soul the immaterial animating essence), having not the Spirit (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44">1Co 15:44</reference>; 1Cor 15:46-48; <reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference>). The unbeliever shall rise with an animal (soul-animated) body, but not like the believer with a spiritual (spirit-endued) body like Christ's (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blameless unto--</hi>rather as Greek, "blamelessly (so as to be in a blameless state) at the coming of Christ." In Hebrew, "peace" and "wholly" (perfect in every respect) are kindred terms; so that the prayer shows what the title "God of peace" implies. Bengel takes "wholly" as collectively, all the Thessalonians without exception, so that no one should fail. And "whole (entire)," individually, each one of them entire, with "spirit, soul, and body." The mention of the preservation of the body accords with the subject (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>). Trench better regards "wholly" as meaning, "having perfectly attained the moral end," namely, to be a full-grown man in Christ. "Whole," complete, with no grace which ought to be wanting in a Christian. <div eID="gen36857" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3290acac20c563b8e3a8948a0d3c9028b14c838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18004"/><div sID="gen36858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18004"/><hi type="bold">24. Faithful--</hi>to His covenant promises (<reference osisRef="John.10.27-John.10.29">Joh 10:27-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.23">10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that calleth you--</hi>God, the caller of His people, will cause His calling not to fall short of its designed end.<div eID="gen36859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do it--</hi>preserve and present you blameless at the coming of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Ro 8:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.10">1Pe 5:10</reference>). You must not look at the foes before and behind, on the right hand and on the left, but to God's faithfulness to His promises, God's zeal for His honor, and God's love for those whom He calls. <div eID="gen36860" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed59cee781387378fcbe0854213f53ab0427258b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18005"/><div sID="gen36861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18005"/>25. Some oldest manuscripts read, "Pray ye also for (literally, 'concerning') us"; make us and our work the subject of your prayers, even as we have been just praying for you (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>). Others omit the "also." The clergy need much the prayers of their flocks. Paul makes the same request in the Epistles to Romans, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon, and in Second Corinthians; not so in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus, whose intercessions, as his spiritual sons, he was already sure of; nor in the Epistles, I Corinthians, and Galatians, as these Epistles abound in rebuke. <div eID="gen36861" type="x-p"/>
entries.574f96a483d31cf13fe14f67f6294d29d26c45c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18006"/><div sID="gen36862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18006"/>26. Hence it appears this Epistle was first handed to the elders, who communicated it to "the brethren."<div eID="gen36862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy kiss--</hi>pure and chaste. "A kiss of charity" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.14">1Pe 5:14</reference>). A token of Christian fellowship in those days (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.7.45">Lu 7:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.37">Ac 20:37</reference>), as it is a common mode of salutation in many countries. The custom hence arose in the early Church of passing the kiss through the congregation at the holy communion [Justin Martyr, Apology, 1.65; Apostolic Constitutions, 2.57], the men kissing the men, and the women the women, in the Lord. So in the Syrian Church each takes his neighbor's right hand and gives the salutation, "Peace." <div eID="gen36863" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bd200ff25eacdddb67a5b16827030823a4ef33d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18007"/><div sID="gen36864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18007"/><hi type="bold">27. I charge--</hi>Greek, "I adjure you."<div eID="gen36864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">read unto all--</hi>namely, publicly in the congregation at a particular time. The Greek aorist tense implies a single act done at a particular time. The earnestness of his adjuration implies how solemnly important he felt this divinely inspired message to be. Also, as this was the FIRST of the Epistles of the New Testament, he makes this the occasion of a solemn charge, that so its being publicly read should be a sample of what should be done in the case of the others, just as the Pentateuch and the Prophets were publicly read under the Old Testament, and are still read in the synagogue. Compare the same injunction as to the public reading of the Apocalypse, the LAST of the New Testament canon (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Re 1:3</reference>). The "all" includes women and children, and especially those who could not read it themselves (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.12">De 31:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.8.33-Josh.8.35">Jos 8:33-35</reference>). What Paul commands with an adjuration, Rome forbids under a curse [Bengel]. Though these Epistles had difficulties, the laity were all to hear them read (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>; even the very young, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>). "Holy" is omitted before "brethren" in most of the oldest manuscripts, though some of them support it. <div eID="gen36865" type="x-p"/>
entries.86e331589e301a31389561efd89046e1cc500dd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18008"/><div sID="gen36866" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18008"/>28. (See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.14">2Co 13:14</reference>.) Paul ends as he began (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.1">1Th 1:1</reference>), with "grace." The oldest manuscripts omit "Amen," which probably was the response of the Church after the public reading of the Epistle.<div eID="gen36866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36867" type="x-p"/> The subscription is a comparatively modern addition. The Epistle was not, as it states, written from Athens, but from Corinth; for it is written in the names of Silas and Timothy (besides Paul), who did not join the apostle before he reached the latter city (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Ac 18:5</reference>).  <chapter eID="1Thess.5"/><div eID="gen36867" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen36571" osisID="1Thess" type="book"/>

entries.309c8eb554a1f356dcb46707e8707e0de3774814: <div eID="gen51211" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51212" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51213" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51213" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51212" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51214" type="x-p"/> The apostle continues to speak of Christ's coming to judgment, and the uncertainty of the time in which it shall take place, and the careless state of sinners, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.1-1Thes.5.3">1Thes 5:1-3</reference>. Shows the Thessalonians that they are children of the light; that they should watch and pray, and put on the armor of God, being called to obtain salvation by Christ, who died for them; that whether dead or alive, when the day of judgment comes, they may live for ever with him; and that they should comfort and edify each other with these considerations, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.4-1Thes.5.11">1Thes 5:4-11</reference>. He exhorts them to remember those who labor among them, and are over them in the Lord; and to esteem such highly for their work's sake, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.12">1Thes 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.13">1Thes 5:13</reference>. He charges them to warn, comfort, and support those who stood in need of such assistance, and to be patient and beneficent towards all, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.14">1Thes 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.15">1Thes 5:15</reference>. He points out their high spiritual privileges; warns them against neglecting or misimproving the gifts of the Spirit, and the means of grace, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.16-1Thes.5.20">1Thes 5:16-20</reference>. They are also exhorted to prove all things; to abstain from all evil; and to expect to be sanctified, through spirit, soul, and body, by him who has promised this, and who is faithful to his promises, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.21-1Thes.5.24">1Thes 5:21-24</reference>. Recommends himself and brethren to their prayers; shows them how they are to greet each other; charges them to read this epistle to all the brethren; and concludes with the usual apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="1Thes.5.25-1Thes.5.28">1Thes 5:25-28</reference>. <div eID="gen51214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51215" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51216" type="x-p"/> But of the times and the seasons - It is natural to suppose, after what he had said in the conclusion of the preceding chapter concerning the coming of Christ, the raising of the dead, and rendering those immortal who should then be found alive, without obliging them to pass through the empire of death, that the Thessalonians would feel an innocent curiosity to know, as the disciples did concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, when those things should take place, and what should be the signs of those times, and of the coming of the Son of man.
