               <ns0:p n="9">9 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 9.22. 1 Pet. 2.8. Jude 4.</ns0:note> God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Some Expositors make these words an argument to all the Duties of Holiness mentioned both in this and the forego<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Chapters, and it is true, that the knowledge of our being Elected, or appointed to Salvation, doth not in the Elect en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage to sin or sloth, as some affirm, but engage to all holiness; but I had rather restrain the words, and that either to the hope of Salvation mentioned immediately before, and then the sence to be this, we may well hope for Salvation seeing God hath ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed us to it, or to his whole discourse about the coming of Christ, and so they may give the reason why the dead in Christ must rise, and must with the Living Saints meet the Lord in the air, and be for ever with him; yea, and why they need not fear the destruction that will come upon others at that day, and why they should be watchful for its coming, because saith the Apostle, God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain Salvation, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> having spoken of two sorts of persons, the Children of the day, and Children of the night, and the sud<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n destruction of the one, and Salvation of the other at the coming of Christ; he here ascends to the first Original of both, which is Gods appointm<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>nt, which is an Act of God's Sove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reign will, determining mens final Estates, which seems to be more than meer praescience, or foreknowledge, an act of Gods mind, as appears by <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.29. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.2. or more than appointing of the means and way of Salvation, but not of persons to be saved, or of persons only materially, as to the number how many, but not formally, or individually who they are that shall be saved; whereas the Apostle writes of some <ns0:hi>whose names are in the book of life, Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.3. and that <ns0:hi>from the foundation of the World. Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.8. and <ns0:hi>chosen before the foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation of the World, Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.4. otherwise every mans Salvation would depend more upon the uncertainty of Mans Will, than the Eternal and immutable Will of God; whereas whatever God works in man's Salvation, is according to the Counsel of his Will, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.11. And Gods Counsel is certain, immutable, and eternal, extending not only to actions and means, but per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.29, 30. neither is this appointment of God grounded upon the foresight of mans Faith; for if Faith be the gift of God, this gift proceeds from Gods counsel and sore-appoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment; else men may say<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> That I may be saved, I must thank God, but that I am saved, I must thank my self. And hence there is a possibility for no man to be saved; and all the coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sels of God in Christ to be made frustrate; but this is no place for controversie, only where God appoints to Salvation, he ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />points also to means, and without the means, there is no at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainment of the end, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.4. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.2. And the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle here makes Salvation stand opposite to Wrath, what before he call'd destruction: <ns0:hi>verse.</ns0:hi> 3. he here calleth Wrath, because Gods Wrath produceth it, and is manifested in it. And those that are saved, are delivered from it, and the supream reason is, because they were not appointed to it, but to Salvation, and none that are appointed to the one, are appointed to the other. The vessels of Wrath and of Mercy are set in an opposite di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stinction, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.22, 23. and so in the Text to illustrate the Mercy of God the more in them that are saved: And whereas the Apostle calls it the <ns0:hi>obtaining</ns0:hi> of Salvation, it implies mans endeavours for it, though he be appointed of God to it, and speaking positively not only of himself, but these believing <ns0:hi>Thes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salonians</ns0:hi> also, <ns0:hi>he hath appointed us to obtain Salvation,</ns0:hi> doth not this also imply that some good assurance of Salvation may be obtained in this World.</ns0:note> by our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Decrees of Salvation are exe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cuted in him, and by him. And <ns0:hi>there is no Salvation in any other, Acts</ns0:hi> 4.12. And he saveth not only by his Doctrine and Example as some have affirmed, but by his blood as the meri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />torious, and his Spirit as the efficient cause of Salvation, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the Infinite Wisdom of God could have found out another way I shall not enquire, but this it hath pitched upon, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in Mercy and Justice are admirably glorified together, and the highest engagement imaginable laid upon men to love, serve, and honour their Creator. And as the freeness of Gods Grace is manifested in his appointing men to Salvation, so the exceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Riches of it in saving them by Jesus Christ. And whereas two things are necessary to it, the reconciling us unto God, and restoring his Image in us: The former we have by the merit of his Blood, and the latter by the operation of his Spirit; so that we have no ground for that fond opinion, That if men walk ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nestly and uprightly, they may be saved in any Religion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 14 8, 9. 2 Cor. 5.16.</ns0:note> Who died for us, that whether we wake or sleep we should live together with him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Some referre these words to the latter end of the foregoing chapter, where the Apostle had spoke of the Saints Death and Resurrection, which is their sleeping and waking as they are here call'd. And their being for ever with the Lord is here called their living together with him. And least it might be thought that none should be with Christ until they awaked at the Resurrection, he therefore speaks of living with Christ even when we sleep. He had spoke of sleep in another sense <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6. as meant of security, but here meant of death, as its taken <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.14. And as watching is set opposite to the former sleep, so here waking to the latter, which is a Resurrection from death. And we hence gather that the Soul doth not sleep with the Body, but lives with the Lord when that sleeps in the Grave. As the Apostle expected to be with the Lord upon the dissolu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of his Body, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 1.23. and he mentions it as the privi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of other Saints as well as his own, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.1. When we sleep we are with him only in our Souls, when we wake we shall be with him both in body and soul. And both these we have from Christs death. If he had not died Heaven had been shut against our Souls, for our entrance into the holiest of all is by his Blood, and the vail of his Flesh rent for us, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.19, 26. and the grave would have shut up our Bodies, and there would have been no Resurrection, so that our living with Christ both when we sleep and when we wake springs out of his death. Others carry these words no further then the foregoing verse shewing <ns0:hi>how</ns0:hi> we are saved by Christ; saith the Apostle, he dyed for us. As God appointed persons to be saved, and Christ to be the person to be saved by, so also to be saved by his death, with respect to his Father he is said to be put to death, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.18. with respect to his own freedom and willingness, he is said here to dye for us. And his dying for us implyeth the greatness of our guilt, and expresseth the greatness of his own love, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 15.13. He loved us, and thereupon would have us live with him, and he dyed that we and he may live together.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And so he may be said to dye for our Salvation, the substance whereof consisteth in our living with him. To live with so glorious a person, and a person that is full of love to us, and shall then be perfectly beloved of us, and that stands in many near relations to us, and whose presence will have such a blessed influence up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on us, and in such a place as heaven <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s, and that for ever, sure carries the substance of our Salvation in it. And if this was the end of his death, sure it was more then to be an example of Faith, Patience, and submission to God. Or to confirm to us the Doctrine he preached; it was to satisfie divine Justice, and obtain the pardon of our <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>in, and merit for us the priviledge of living with him.</ns0:note>

The Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle had laid before them many comfortable truths; which they were to comfort one another by; and if we read the words, <ns0:hi>ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hort one another,</ns0:hi> it referrs to the necessary duties of Religion he had mentioned in this and the foregoing chapter.</ns0:note>, and edifie one another <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">And this follows from both the former, as alluding to an house that is built up by degrees; and so is every Church the house of God; and consisting of living stones, every part is to seek the build<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing up of the whole.                   </ns0:note> even as also ye do <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">And what the Apostle exhorted them to, they were already in the practise of; for which he here again commends them as he had done upon several accounts before, not to flatter but to en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage them to proceed, and to set before other Churches their example for imitation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

In civil respects, when men live without a calling, or being in it, neglect it, or in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trude into other mens business, and perform not the Duties of their Civil Relations. 2.                      </ns0:gap> an allu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion to such as lift at one end of the burden, to help to bear it, answering to the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.26. <ns0:hi>The Spirit helpeth our infirmities:</ns0:hi> And the weak are either the weak in Knowledge, weak in Faith, that understand not their own Liberty in the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.1. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.9. The word signifies Longanimity, or Long-suffering, and is often attributed to God, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 34.6. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.22. It consisteth in the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferring, or moderating of anger, to wait without anger when men delay us, and to suffer without undue anger when they deal injuriously with us, whether they be good men or evil, believers or infidels, the strong or the weak, Ministers or People.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 17.13. and 24.29. 1 Cor. 6.7.</ns0:note> See that none render evil for evil unto any man <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">These words seem directed to the guides of the Church, who are called Overseers, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.28. and therefore the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle requires them to <ns0:hi>see</ns0:hi> that none render evil, &c. Or if to the whole Church as before, then it is a solemn charge which they ought to be all circumspect in observing. And the charge is first negative not to render evil for evil; which is to revenge themselves; and that is forbidden by the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.17, 19. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.9. And is the resisting of evil, forbidden by our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.39. But is to be understood of pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate revenge rising out of malice, not of publick censures ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Civil and Ecclesiastical. Or of seeking reparations for inju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries received in Courts of Justice according to Law and Equity. This private revenge cannot consist with that patience that he required towards all men in the foregoing verse, nor is it con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formable to the example of Christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.23. nor to the Christian calling and profession, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.21. 2. Positive, good in it self, or that which is good to others as the word is often taken, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.11. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.53. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.6. and so stands opposite here to the rendring of evil. And the word <ns0:hi>follow,</ns0:hi> signifies an earnest following, which is sometimes taken in a bad sense, for persecution, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.11. and sometimes in a good sense, as 1 <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.14. <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.11. and to follow good imports more then only to do good, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.11. when the inward bent of the Soul, and the outward endeavours are to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards doing good. And this ought to be <ns0:hi>ever,</ns0:hi> or always, that is in all places, times, occasions, company. Mans course of Life ought in this to be uniform, though his outward condition vary. Sometime to do good to the Souls, sometimes to the Bodies of men, and that either in a privative or positive good; prevent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing evil, or bestowing that which is good.</ns0:note>: but ever <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 6.10.</ns0:note> follow that which is good <ns0:hi>i,</ns0:hi> both among your selves, and to all men <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Do good to all, and especially to the houshold of Faith, Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.10. As they say of good<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the commoner the better, but the contrary of evil, Christians stand in a special relation to one another, but in a common relation to all, and every Relation ought to be filled up with good. As love is a common debt to all men, so the fruit of it which is doing good. Our doing good should not be confined among Christians only of one way, opinion, or congregation, nor to men only under some limiting circumstan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, but it should reach all men as we have ability, opportuni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, and call; even Enemies themselves, as our Saviour requires <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.44. This is to act like God, and may commend Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligion to all men, and is not to be lookt upon as commended by way of counsel as the Papists say, but commanded by precept. And it is not enough not to do evil, but we must do good, not to save a mans Life when we have power to do it, is to kill him, as Christ argues <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 3.4. so not to save a mans estate, when we may, is to steal from him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:521" />16 Rejoyce evermore. <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Here the Apostle adds more Christian duties, briefly ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prest, and set close one to another, and they seem to have a mutual connexion, but not so relative to others as those before mentioned, but personal to themselves. He begins with the duty of Rejoycing, joy is an affection of the Soul springing from the hope or possession of some suitable good. And it is either natural, which is common to men with beasts, arising from that good that is suitable to their several natures. Or spiritual, which is Joy wrought by the Spirit, and exercised upon spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual objects. And this the Apostle here means, and is called re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joycing in the Lord, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.4. and the joy of the Holy Ghost, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.17. arising either from what spiritual good we alrea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy possess, or hope to possess, <ns0:hi>exhibita & promissa, Bernard.</ns0:hi> which is there upon called a rejoycing in hope, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.2. and 12.12. The Apostle speaks here of the duty indefinitely, onely requires it to be <ns0:hi>evermore,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.4. Though God sometimes calls to mourning, yet its no where said mourn evermore, because rejoycing ought to be in a more constant practise, and all spiritual mourning tends to it, and will end in it; and he commends it as seasonable to these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> to support them under their present sufferings. The grounds of a Christians Joy alwayes abide, and he is not only to retain it in the habit, but to mix it with all his sorrows, and sufferings, as 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.6. <ns0:hi>Ye greatly rejoyce though for a season in heaviness.</ns0:hi> Whereas carnal mirth is mixt with sadness, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 14.13. So that a Christian ought to rejoyce in every condition, not only in prosperity but adversity, and especially when called to suffer for Righteousness sake, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.12. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.13. It is not only allowed but commanded. This joy is one great part of Gods Kingdom even in this World, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.17. much more in the World to come. And therefore the Apostle speaks of rejoycing evermore, whereas mourning is but for a time, and ends to the Saints in this Life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Pray <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This is a means to maintain our rejoycing, and therefore next mentioned. Prayer is a making known our requests to God, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.6. And it is either mental in the heart only, as <ns0:hi>Hannahs</ns0:hi> was; or vocal, exprest with the voice: or as some add, vital; so good works have a voice to bring down bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sings, as mens sins cry for vengeance.</ns0:note> without ceasing <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not as the <ns0:hi>Euchites</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Messalians,</ns0:hi> of old, who hence thought no other duties were required, but alwayes Praying; but by the word in the Text, is either meant a praying without fainting, as in the parable, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.1. and which the Apostle calls a perseverance in prayer, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.18. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.2. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, or praying with strength, as the greek word there imports, and so not to faint, so <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.12. Or a praying in every thing, as <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.6. <ns0:hi>In every thing let your request be made known,</ns0:hi> &c. Or, <ns0:hi>in every sea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.18. to take hold of the seasons of prayer. Or, in all seasons and times whether good or bad, yet still to pray. And all this is meant by the word in the Text, which is also used <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.9. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.3. and 2.13. and implies in ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral no more but a constant course of prayer, so <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. to watch unto prayer as that the course of it be not interrupt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by any diversions. As also to preserve an heart disposed to pray at all times: and to mingle ejaculatory prayers with the several actions of our lives, our wants are continual and God will be acknowledged in all our supplies, and therefore we ought to pray continually.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.20.</ns0:note> In every thing give thanks <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">When we have obtained mercy by Prayer, then we are to give thanks, and what ever we may pray for, that we ought to give thanks for. And so by that understand and limit the gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral expression in the Text. We are not to give thanks when we fall into sin, for that we ought not to pray for. Yet if we have the pardon of it, or get any good by it, we should then give thanks; and so may be said concerning affliction, we are to give thanks in every condition, either of prosperity or ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versity. And with all our supplications, we are joyn thanks<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />givings, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.6. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.2. and thanksgiving properly re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fers to some mercy received<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> whether privative, or positive, tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poral, or spiritual, private or publick, and we are in all these to give thanks. Though praising God may reach further, which is to adore the excellencies of his being as they are glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious in themselves, or the excellencies of his works as they are in themselves praise worthy. And Thanksgiving for mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy received is. 1. A taking notice of it as coming from God. 2. Setting a due value upon it. 3. A sense of Gods goodness and our own unworthiness. 4. Praising him for it.</ns0:note>: for this is the will of God <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Some car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry this as a motive to all the preceding duties, but rather to this last mentioned: As if this was in special the Will of God; being a duty so much to his own glory and our good, and by will we must by a Metonymye understand the thing willed, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.6. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.12. It is required by the Law of nature not written, which is part of Gods will. The Heathen are reprov<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for not being thankful, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.21. and they made Laws to punish it, and accounted it the greatest reproach, <ns0:hi>ingratum si dixeris omnia dixeris,</ns0:hi> and by the Law of God that is written. The moral Law requires it, and the Ceremonial Law required offerings by way of thanksgiving; which we call gratulatory. And the Gospel requires it, it being one of the Gospel Sacrifices <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.15. and pleaseth the Lord better then the greatest of the legal Sacrifices, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 69.30, 31. and it being said to be the Will of God in the Text, it must needs be pleasing to him.</ns0:note> in Christ Jesus concerning you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either meant as this will of his is signified to us by him, not only by the Law of nature, or of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> but by Christ Jesus, and so it may be of greater force upon Christians, and hereby it is to be looked upon as one of the Commandements of Christ also. Or we may understand it upon the account of Christ, and the great love of God in him. Though thanks<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />giving is due for the least mercy, yet Gods will especially re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quires it with respect to Christ. And so especially of Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians who partake of Christ, and the Love of God in him: as the Apostle here adds, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>towards you</ns0:hi> in special, the Heathens were obliged to thankfulness for Rain from Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, and fruitful seasons, these common blessings; much more are Christians for the special blessings they receive by Christ Jesus.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 4.30. see 1 Cor. 14.30.</ns0:note> Quench not the spirit <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That ye may be enabled to pray and give thanks, as before, <ns0:hi>Quench not the Spirit.</ns0:hi> And by the figure <ns0:hi>Meiosis</ns0:hi> he means che<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rish the spirit. The spirit is compared to Fire, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.11. and he came down upon the Apostles in the similitude of tongues of Fire, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 2.3. but the spirit himself cannot be quenched, he means it therefore of his gifts and operations. Which are either ordinary or extraordinary. Many had extraordinary gifts in the primitive times of healing, tongues, government pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesie, &c. those that had them, without question, should have taken care not, by any fault of their own, to lose them. Especial<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly that of prophesie, which the Apostle prefers before all others, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.1. and mentions here in the following verse. And which the Apostle exhorted <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> to stir up in himself, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.6. As we stir up the Fire to quicken it, so the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> imports. The like is required of Ministers with respect to their Ministerial gifts which are now given, but there are ordinary gifts and operations of the Spirits common to all Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians. As enlightning, quickening, sanctifying, comforting the Soul, men by sloth, security, earthly incumbrances, inor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinate affections, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ay abate these operations of the Spirit, which the Apostle calls the quenching it, the fire upon the Altar was kept always burning by the care of the Priests. Fire will go out either by neglecting it, or casting water upon it. By not exercising Grace in the duties of Religion, or by allowing sin in our selves we may quench the Spirit. As appears in <ns0:hi>David, Psal.</ns0:hi> 51.10, 11, 12. Not that the Habits of grace may be totally extinguish'd in the truly regenerate, yet they may be abated as to degree, and lively exercise. Yet those common illuminations, and convictions of the Spirit which persons <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />regenerate especially such that live under the Gospel do often find, may be totally lost, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.4, 5, 6. and we read of Gods Spirit ceasing to strive with the old World, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 6.3. and the Scribes and Pharisees resisting the Holy Ghost, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 7.51. which were not persons regenerate. He may sometimes strive with men, but not overcome them; and there is a quenching of the Spirit in others as well as our selves; people may quench it in their Ministers by discouraging them, and in one another by bad examples or reproaching the Zeal, and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wardness that they see in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Despise not prophesyings <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Thereby we may quench the Spirit, which usually works upon mens Minds and Hearts by it. By prophesie is sometimes meant foretelling things to come, and speaking by extraordinary Revelation, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.29, 30. sometimes the Scriptures are so call'd, especially the old Testament, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.21. and sometimes the interpretation and applying of Scripture, which is the same that we now call preaching, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.3. And the duty with respect to it, is not to despise it, to set it at nought as a thing of no worth. The word is often used in the New Testament, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.9. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.3.10. But the Apostle useth again the figure Meiosis before mentioned, and means, Prize, Value, and highly esteem it, attend upon it, have great regard to it. It being an ordinance of God for In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction and Edification, yea, and for Conversion also, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.24, 25. some despise it because of the outward meanness of the persons which prophesie, some through a proud conceit of their own knowledge, some by a contempt of Religion it self. These <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> had been commended for their great profici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ency, and yet were still to attend upon prophesying in the Church. Which he calls prophesyings in the plural number, referring either to the several Prophets that prophesied, or to the several parts of their prophesie, or the times they prophesied. And the Prophets were either such as prophesied only by an extraor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary gift, and immediate revelation, which some private mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers of the Church, had in those times, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.29, 30. Or such as prophesied not only by gift, but office also, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.11.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:521" />21 <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 2.11.</ns0:note> Prove all things <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This duty relates to the former; as they were to attend up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on prophesyings so to exercise a discerning judgment about what was prophesied. For <ns0:hi>all things</ns0:hi> is not to be taken here universally, but for Doctrines and Opinions in Religion which were delivered by the Prophets. The same which the Apostle <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> requires, <ns0:hi>beleive not every spirit but try the spirits,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and its the same word there which in this Text we read <ns0:hi>prove</ns0:hi>; alluding to Gold or other Mettals which are tryed in the Fire, or by a touch-stone, as some think. And though there was a peculiar gift of discerning of Spirits, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.10. yet it is the duty of every Christian to try mens Spirits and Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrines whether from God or no. The Apostle speaks here to the Saints in general, and so doth the Apostle St. <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 4.1. And mens Doctrines are to be judged of by the Scriptures as the standard of Truth, as the <ns0:hi>Bereans</ns0:hi> were commended for searching the Scriptures about the Apostles Doctrine, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 17.11. and the Apostle prayes for the <ns0:hi>Philippians</ns0:hi> that they might discern things that differ, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 1.10. and if they had not yet attained it as they ought, yet he prays that they might, and not be alwayes, <ns0:hi>babes, but such</ns0:hi> as the Apostle speaks of, <ns0:hi>who have their senses exercised in the discerning of good and evil, Heb.</ns0:hi> 5. 13, 14. the people are to look upon them as their guides and leaders, as they are called <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.7.17. and such as are to go before them in the searching and dispensing of truth, yet because the best are but infallible, they ought to try their Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine by the rule of Truth. Which is that judgment of discretion which Protestants allow to the people in their disputes with the Papists against their Doctrine of Infallibility, and implicit Faith, which grounds the peoples Faith upon the Authority of Men, which ought to rest upon the authority of God. As we ought not easily to reject the authority and Faith of the Church, so not to believe with a blind Faith, or obey with a blind obedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence.</ns0:note>, hold fast that which is good <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The good here meant is Truth, which is an intellectu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al good, the contrary to which is Error, which is a mental evil. When we have proved mens Doctrines and Opinions, what we find agreeable to the Scriptures of Truth we ought to hold fast. And though all Truth hath a goodness in it, yet especially di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Truth, and the Doctrine of the Gospel, which the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle calls, <ns0:hi>That good thing</ns0:hi> committed to <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.14. It is good with respect to the soul, and so better then any bodily good, and good that refers to eternity, and so better then any temporal good. Now this good we are to <ns0:hi>hold fast.</ns0:hi> To hold it fast against adversaries and all opposition as some understand the word, to hold it as with both hands, against seducing Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine, Satans Temptations, and the Worlds Persecution. The same word is used concerning the good ground that held fast the seed of the Word, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 8.15. So 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.2. we are to retain the Truth, but not detain it, as the heathen are said to do, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.18. where we find also the same word as in the Text. It is a duty much prest by the Apostles in their E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pistles to the Saints and Churches that had received the Gospel that they would hold fast, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.13. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.9. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 4.14. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.13<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 25, and 3.3. And there is holding fast the Truth, as well in Practise as Opinion, and which may be the ground of the name formerly given to such as opposed the Er<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rors of Antichrist before the word <ns0:hi>Protestant</ns0:hi> was known, call'd <ns0:hi>Fast-men.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 4.8.</ns0:note> Abstain from all appearance of evil <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To make this verse have its connection with the former, some Expositors understand it of Doctrines and Opinions only. To take heed of Opinions that seem erroneous, and not rashly to receive them without due examination. Though this sence is not to be excluded, yet the verse need not be confined to it, but to extend to practise also; as in Worship to abstain from the shew of Idolatry, as to eat meat in an Idols Temple was not alwaies gross Idolatry, but had some appearance of it; and therefore the Apostle forbids it, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.14. And so in Civil Conversation, not only to abstain from vice, but the ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance of it; as of Pride, Covetousness, Drunkenness, Whore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and that both with respect to our selves, lest by ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turing upon that which hath some shew of evil, we step into the evil it self, and with respect to others, that we may not occasion the taking offence though not justly given; or do that which may any way encourage a real evil in them by that appea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance of it, which they see in our selves; yet we ought not upon this account to forbear the discharge of any necessary Duty. Some read the words, <ns0:hi>Abstain from all kind of evil,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is so used by Logicians: But here to insist on particulars is infinite. And thus the Apostle con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cludes all these positive Duties with a general praecept which he leaves with them at the close of his Epistle; having dehorted them from many evils, now he exhorts them to abstain from the appearance of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 4.9.</ns0:note> the very God of peace <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 3.13.</ns0:note> sanctifie you wholly <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Apostle here concludes all with Prayer, as knowing all his exhortations and admonitions before given would not be effectual without God, and he prays for their sanctification and preservation, Though they were sanctified already, yet but in part, so that he prays for further progress in it to perfection, which he means by <ns0:hi>wholly.</ns0:hi> A word no where used by the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle, but in this place, and variously rendred; some render it <ns0:hi>thro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ghout,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>perfectly,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>in every part,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> all things,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>fully,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>French entirely</ns0:hi>: It may refer to all the parts of holiness, and the degrees of holiness, and to the whole man in the several faculties of Soul and Body, exprest in the next words by <ns0:hi>Spirit, Soul,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Body,</ns0:hi> that their whole man may be entirely separated, and consecrated to God, offered up to him as a Sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.1, and hence we observe that not only the beginning, but progress in Grace is from God. The Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle therefore prays for it to God, (whom he calls the God of peace, to enforce his exhortation to peace, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3) which con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />futes the Pelagians, who thought objective Grace sufficient to sanctifie, or that mans Nature needs only at first to be exci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted by God, and then can go forward of it self, being only maimed, not totally corrupted by the fall. It's true, our facul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties cooperate with God, but not of themselves, but as acted by h<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s inherent Grace, and indwelling Spirit. And what the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle prays for, that Christians should endeavour after, which is a progress in sanctification to perfection. We may also note, That true sanctification reacheth to the whole man, Spirit, Soul and Body. 2. Preservation, which we call perseverance, exprest here both by the Subject and Term of it. The Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject is the whole man, branched into three parts, <ns0:hi>Spirit, Soul,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Body,</ns0:hi> figured, at least resembled by the three parts of the Temple. Consider man naturally, and then by Spirit we mean his superiour faculties, as the Mind, Conscience, Rational Will. By Soul, his sensitive Appetite, with the Affections and Passi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons. By Body, the outward Man, the Tabernacle and Instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of the soul. The <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Rabbins and others think all these are exprest in the Creation of man, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2.7. <ns0:hi>God formed man of the dust of the earth,</ns0:hi> there is his Body, <ns0:hi>and breathed into man the breath of life,</ns0:hi> or lives, <ns0:hi>Nishmath Chaiim, Nephesh Chaijah</ns0:hi>; that is, the faculties of the rational Soul, and Man became a living Soul, that is, the Animal and Sensitive Life; neither is pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly meant here the Spirit of God, for he saith, your Spirit, nor the sanctified part of the Soul; for he prays for the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serving of their persons. Only observe when he speaks of their Spirit, he calls it their <ns0:hi>whole Spirit.</ns0:hi> And by the Figure <ns0:hi>Zeug<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ma</ns0:hi> the word <ns0:hi>whole</ns0:hi> is to be carryed also to Soul and Body, so that as he prayed their whole Man might be sanctified, so their whole Spirit, their whole Soul, their whole Body might be preserved; and the same word we find <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 1.4. where it is rendred <ns0:hi>perfect,</ns0:hi> alluding to the perfect possessing of an Inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance, or lot that belongs to a man. And by preserving, he means not so much the substance of the Spirit, Soul, and Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy, to preserve them in Being, as to preserve them in Holiness. And they are preserved, partly by being delivered from the sinful Distempers that are naturally in them; as ignorance, Vanity, Impotency, and Enmity in the mind, Reluctancy and Obstinacy in the Will, Inordinacy and Irregularity in the Af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections; Disobedience to the Law of God, and the Regular Commands of the Soul in the Body. If these prevail, they will bring destruction: as Diseases prevailing destroy the Natural Life; and partly also by being supplyed with that Grace where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by they act regularly towards God, and are serviceable to the end of mans Being, as supply of Oyl preserveth the Lamp burn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing: And whereby we may understand, that not only the Infe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riour Faculties are corrupted in mans fall, but the superiour and the supreme of all, else the Apostle need not have prayed for the Spirit to be sanctified and preserved as well as the Soul and Body. And elsewhere prays for a renewing in the Spirit of the Mind, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.23.</ns0:note>: and I <ns0:hi>pray God</ns0:hi> your whole Spirit, and soul and body be preserved <ns0:hi>z</ns0:hi> blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Next we may consider this preservation with respect to the term of it, <ns0:hi>Preserved blameless unto the coming of Christ.</ns0:hi> The same which the Apostle means by <ns0:hi>being preserved to Gods Heavenly Kingdom,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.18. and 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.14. And those that are preserved to that day, are preserved to the end, and will be found blameless and their whole Man, Spirit, Soul, and Body be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing first sanctified, and then preserved, shallbe saved and glorified. And the Apostle insinuates in the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>blameless,</ns0:hi> that strict discovery that will be made of persons at that day, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in some will be blamed, and others be found without blame. And herein the Apostle may have respect both to the Teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers and Ministers in this Church, and the private Members of it, that with respect to their several Duties belonging to them they may be found blameless; and though according to the strictness of the Law of God, none can be without blame, yet, those that have been sincere, and have their sin pardoned, and their persons accepted in Christ may be found blameless in the day of Christ, however it is that which we should strive after.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Thess. 3.3.</ns0:note> 24 Faithful <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that calleth you, who also will do <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">We had in the former verse the Apostles Prayer, here his Faith; and he speaks it by way of consolation to them, that what he had prayed for, God would effect; what need he then have prayed? Because Gods Decrees and Promises though immutable, and infallible, yet are to be accomplisht in a way of Prayer. Prayer is our Duty, and Gods Decrees and Promises are no dispensation from our Duty: Besides, Duties are more known to us than Gods Decrees. And God decrees the means as well as the end. But what is it he saith God will do? It is not here exprest, and the word, <ns0:hi>It,</ns0:hi> it not in the Original, but only <ns0:hi>God will do,</ns0:hi> God will effect. He had prayed God would sacrifie them wholly, and preserve them blameless, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And this he would do or effect. And he grounds his confidence partly upon Gods calling them. For the Apostle knew that Gods Gifts and Calling are without Repentance, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.30. and 11.29. <ns0:hi>And whom he called, them <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e justified, and glorified.</ns0:hi> And this the Apostle saw in these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> by that efficacy of the Gospel upon their hearts, that they were effectually cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led and chosen, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.4. whence he concluded they should be at last wholly sanctified, and finally preserved, which is a strong argument against final Apostacy from a state of Grace. Though many that are outwardly called are never sanctified, much less wholly. But of this Call the Apostle speaks not here, at least not only. And partly also upon Gods faithfulness, who had called them. He doth not say, God is able to do it, though that is true, but he is faithful, and will do it. Those that are effectually called are brought into Gods Covenant, where perfection and perseverance are promised, and Gods faithfulness obligeth him to make good his Covenant. It is an Act of Grace and Mercy to call men, but when called, Gods faithfulness is ingaged to preserve them, and perfect the work begun, as 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.8. The Apostle tells the <ns0:hi>Corinthians, God will confirm them, to the end they might be blameless in the day of Christ,</ns0:hi> and his argument is, for God is faithful by whom ye were cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, <ns0:hi>&c. ver.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:522" />25 Brethren, pray for us <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Apostle a little before had prayed for them, now he begs Prayers of them as he doth of other Churches, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.30. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.3. Ministers and People need each others Prayers, and it is a mutual Duty they owe to one another. Ministers are obliged by special Office, People by Common duty; with re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect to the success of the Gospel in general, 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 3.1. and their own edification by their labours. The Apostle, as he did not think it below him to call these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians,</ns0:hi> Brethren, so neither to beg their prayers. Those that stand highest in the Church, may stand in need of the meanest and lowest. The head cannot say to the foot, I have no need of thee. Those that preach not the Gospel, may yet promote it by their Prayers; yet this gives no warrant to beg the Prayers of Saints departed, for which we have no precept, promise, or ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample as we have for the other. And what is without faith is sin. It is at the best doubtful whether they know our state be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low, or can hear us when we pray, and certainly God never required us to pray upon such uncertainties, and it cannot be in Faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Greet all the brethren <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Apostle concludes several of his Epistles with Greet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, or Salutations, as men usually do at this day, sometimes with salutations from himself alone, sometimes from others; ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther particular Persons, or Churches which he sometimes names as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.6, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.19. and sometimes commends to the Saints their saluting one another, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.20. so here in the Text. The Persons to be saluted are <ns0:hi>all the Brethren,</ns0:hi> that is, all Believers incorporated into the Gospel Church under one common Head, and common Father. More particularly those of this particular Church, we call men Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren, sometimes upon a Natural, sometimes a Civil account, and why not much more upon a Spiritual account. And as their love should reach to the Brotherhood, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.17. so their salutation should reach all the Brethren, Poor, and Rich, High, and Low, Bond, and Free.</ns0:note> with an holy kiss <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, The Right or Ceremony of men kissing each other, was much used among the Jews, and in the Eastern Countries, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27.26. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 24.26. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 7.45. in their salutations; and thence it came to be practis'd in the Churches of Christ as an outward symbol and token of love and freindship. Which is not now practis'd with us amongst men, but is of the same signification with joyning of hands. The uniting of the Lips or Hands toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther denoting the inward conjunction of the heart. The word in the Greek signifies love or friendship, and call'd a kiss of Charity, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>last.</ns0:hi> And though the Ceremony is ceased, yet that which it signified is to be preserved in all Churches, Places and Ages. It was practis'd in the time of <ns0:hi>Iustin Martyr, Iust. Mar. Apolog.</ns0:hi> 2. and <ns0:hi>Tertullian, Tertul. de Oratione</ns0:hi>; and called <ns0:hi>Osculum pacis, A kiss of peace</ns0:hi>; and used especially at their meeting together at the Lords Supper; their Love Feasts, and other solemn assemblies. Its call'd an <ns0:hi>Holy Kiss</ns0:hi>; to distinguish it from the Treacherous Kiss of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> or the Lustful Kiss of the Harlot, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 7.13. And why it is not used Among us now, we need say only, as concerning washing of Feet also, <ns0:hi>we have no such custom nor the Churches of Christ.</ns0:hi> Or as the Apostle speaks, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.8. whatsoever things are lovely, and whatsoever things are of good report, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 I <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>adjure.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> charge you by the Lord <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Apostle having now finish'd the Epistle, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ays a so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lemn charge upon them all, especially their Elders and Tea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chers to have this Epistle published. He now being himself hindred from preaching to them, he sends this Epistle to them to be read to all. He wrote it for publick use, and therefore would have none Ignorant of it, whereby they might all under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand what he had wrote about his great love and care of them, and the commendations he had given of them, and the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structions, Admonitions, Exhortations, and Comforts that were contained therein, of great use to them all: And his charge herein is in a way of Ad<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>uration, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, imposing it on them as by an Oath, as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> did upon his Servant in the case of providing a Wife for <ns0:hi>Isaac. Gen.</ns0:hi> 24.3. And so the High Priest said to Christ, <ns0:hi>I adjure thee by the living God, &c. Mat.</ns0:hi> 26.63, Answering to the Hebrew word, <ns0:hi>hi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>h<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bagnti, I adjure you, Cant.</ns0:hi> 5.8. <ns0:hi>I Charge you, O ye daughters of Ierusalem, &c.</ns0:hi> It imports the requiring of a thing in the Name and Authority of God, with a denunciation of Venge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance if it be not done.</ns0:note>, that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">And all this charge is about the reading of this Epistle, as he commands the Epistle to the <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lossians</ns0:hi> to be read in the Church of the <ns0:hi>Laodiceans, Col.</ns0:hi> 4.16. and that from <ns0:hi>Laodicea</ns0:hi> to be read to them, but not with that Solemn charge as this is. Hence we may gather the Duty of reading the Scriptures in the Church Assemblies; as the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> was read in the Synagogues. And very early in the Christian Churches there were some appointed to be Readers. <ns0:hi>Iulian</ns0:hi> the Apostate was a Reader in the Church at <ns0:hi>Nicomedia.</ns0:hi> And if this was the first Epistle Writ by the Apostle, as some suppose it, he lays this solemn charge first for the reading of this, to shew the duty of the several Churches to the rest of the Scriptures, as they should come to their hand. The word of God should dwell richly and plentifully in the people, and therefore reading it is necessary, together with expounding and applying it. And we hence also may prove against the Papists, it ought to be made known to the people, even all the holy Brethren, and not confined to the Clergy; and to be read in their own Tongue; for so without question was this Epistle read in a language which the people understood. The Apostle was not for confining of Knowledge, and keeping the People in Igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance, as those are who make it the Mother of Devotion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Having exhorted them to salute one another, he now sends them his own Salutation. Not in a Lip-complement as the Mode now is, but in a serious expression of the desire of his Soul: And this, or words to the same purpose are his Salutati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on in every Epistle, which he makes to be his Token, 2 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 3. 17. And by Grace here he means favour, and good Will ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther than inherent Grace. And all blessings which spring from Grace, as sometimes all are comprehended under the word <ns0:hi>Peace.</ns0:hi> Yet Grace and Peace are sometimes in his Salutations both joyn'd together. And though here Christ is only menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned, yet in many other places God the Father is mention'd with him, 2 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 1.2. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.2. Yea, and God the Holy Ghost also 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.14. and where they are not mentioned, yet are all to be understood; for in all works <ns0:hi>ad extra</ns0:hi> they cooperate. And because Grace is so eminently manifested in the whole work of our Salvation, therefore the Apostle doth still mention it in all his Salutations. And with this he con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cludes this Epistle, and with this St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> concludes the whole Bible, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 22. <ns0:hi>ult.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, Amen <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">And the Seal added, not to shut up, but confirm the whole, is, Amen. And is added, as the Voice of the whole Church upon reading the Epistle, as some think, and not by the Apostle himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:div type="part">
                  <ns0:head>¶ The first <ns0:hi>epistle</ns0:hi> unto the Thessalonians was written from Athens.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>These Postscripts to the Apostles Epistles are judged to be added by some Scribes that copied them out, and not by the Apostle himself, as might be made evident; and they are not found in any Epistles but in St. <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> alone. But as it is usual to date Letters from the places where they are writ, so is this dated from <ns0:hi>Athens.</ns0:hi> Hither he was conducted by some bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren after his Persecution at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Berea, Act.</ns0:hi> 17.15. and here we read he stay'd for some time; but that from thence he wrote this Epistle, either then, or any time after, is but conjecture, its more probable he wrote it from <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> because he sends it from <ns0:hi>Timotheus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Silvanus,</ns0:hi> as well as from himself, and they came to him from <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> when he was at <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 18.5.</ns0:p>
